scenarios.title: Join the second wave only after checking possession
scenarios.objective: Assess an offensive activation while keeping a stated covering defender.
scenarios.briefing: F1 has recovered the puck and carries into the neutral zone. YOU are the supporting defender; D2 stays deeper by agreement. F2 is ahead and Gold 3 is recovering near YOU. The drill permits an activation only after secure possession and available support are checked. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The briefing assigns deeper cover to D2 before the activation is considered.

questions.prompt: Which defender has the explicitly stated deeper-cover role?

options.text: Gold 3
D2
YOU

questions.explanation: The briefing assigns deeper cover to D2 before the activation is considered.

questions.prompt: Choose two checks for joining the attack.

options.text: F1’s quality of possession
The idea that every recovery requires both defenders to go
Whether D2 and recovering pressure support the decision

questions.explanation: Activation is a conditional choice; the source principle does not erase risk.

questions.prompt: Arrange an activation assessment.

options.text: Confirm controlled possession
Check covering support and Gold 3
Join or hold according to the updated picture

questions.explanation: Confirming controlled possession and checking covering support/Gold 3 can overlap as YOU skate; only joining or holding has to come last, once both reads are in. The routine assumes the stated cover plan and still needs realistic timing.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a second-wave supporting lane.
questions.explanation: The example is behind F2 and F3 but slightly ahead of carrier F1, in a different lane. Recheck D2’s cover and Gold 3; arrival timing and a passing window are not established.

questions.prompt: F1 bobbles the puck as Gold 3 accelerates. What deserves a fresh decision?

options.text: The old activation regardless of possession
A belief that D2 can cover every possible turnover alone
Whether to hold or recover instead of continuing up ice

questions.explanation: Possession quality and pressure changed, so the original support choice may no longer fit.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a useful second wave from leaving the play without cover?
questions.explanation: Discuss secure possession, D2’s role, pressure and a reachable support lane.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate before joining the second wave?

options.text: F1 has control and D2 is behind me; call if either changes
The attack makes cover unnecessary
F2 owns the puck

questions.explanation: The message names carrier and cover, the two conditions for activation.

questions.prompt: Which two changes require reassessing the activation?

options.text: F1 loses control
D2 leaves the deeper cover
F2 stays wide

questions.explanation: Possession and cover determine whether the second wave remains responsible.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a second-wave lane behind F1, separate from F3.
questions.explanation: The example stays behind F1 and separate from F3. Check D2’s deeper cover and Gold 3’s recovery before continuing; no open pass is guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Gold 3 accelerates as F1 bobbles. What is your new priority?
questions.explanation: Recover or hold the cover first, then re-read F1 and F2. The earlier activation plan is stale.

scenarios.title: Prepare the first touch but keep a second option
scenarios.objective: Compare a prepared first-touch play with the need to update a changed lane.
scenarios.briefing: D1 has released a firm pass toward YOU in the neutral zone. The puck is in transit. F1 is the prepared forward option, but Gold 1 is closing that route. The coach asks YOU to scan before reception; a one-touch pass is permitted, not required. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The loose marker represents the explicitly stated pass in transit.

sources.use: Supports the stated coaching principle. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

scenarios.limits: International U20 coach observation adapted to U18. The source does not validate a universal one-touch rule or this original pass geometry. Static setup: no skating speed, interception timing or uniquely optimal route has been validated. Positional references are examples, not scored targets.

questions.prompt: What is the puck doing according to the briefing?

options.text: Travelling from D1 toward YOU
Already controlled by F1
Already sitting still at YOUR feet

questions.explanation: The loose marker represents the explicitly stated pass in transit.

questions.prompt: Which two cues should affect the first-touch option?

options.text: A requirement to pass first-time regardless
Whether Gold 1 closes F1’s route
The arriving pass quality

questions.explanation: Preparation enables an early option, but a changed route or difficult reception can require another action.

questions.prompt: Arrange a prepared-reception routine.

options.text: Scan the forward option before arrival
Update the lane and puck quality
Redirect or control according to what remains available

questions.explanation: Repeated scans can overlap with receiving; extra control is not automatically an error.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a different receiving angle toward F1 and F2.
questions.explanation: The example changes both forward routes and moves farther from the current loose puck. Whether the pass reaches this new point in time is not established; YOU do not yet control it.

questions.prompt: Gold 1 closes F1 completely as the pass arrives. What might be appropriate?

options.text: Pretend the pre-scan picture cannot change
Control or use another checked option
One-touch into F1’s closed lane by rule

questions.explanation: The latest cue should override a stale preplanned pass.

questions.prompt: How can a player prepare early without committing too early?
questions.explanation: Describe a provisional option, renewed scanning and an alternative if pressure or the arriving puck changes.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate before the loose pass arrives?

options.text: I am preparing a touch; call if F1 or F2 becomes covered
The planned spot guarantees the reception
Both support lanes remain available after Gold closes one route

questions.explanation: The message prepares early while leaving the first touch conditional.

questions.prompt: Which two changes affect the first touch?

options.text: Gold 1 closes F1
F2 remains reachable
The intended puck spot stays current after it drifts

questions.explanation: Pressure and support affect the actual loose puck; the intended spot is no longer enough.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare another approach to the arriving pass.
questions.explanation: The example moves farther from the current puck and closer to Gold 1. Recheck the pass trajectory and pressure before trying this point; it does not guarantee reception or an open outlet.

questions.prompt: Gold closes F1 completely as the puck arrives. Explain your branch.
questions.explanation: Protect the first touch and check F2 or a reset. Do not treat the covered target as the only continuation.

scenarios.title: Manage a lead in the final minute
scenarios.objective: Use the stated clock and score to weigh controlled possession against a safe reset.
scenarios.briefing: Navy leads 3–2 with one minute left. Navy attacks the Gold net. YOU own the puck near centre; F1 is wide support, F2 is higher, and Gold pressures from both sides. The score and clock are explicit practice conditions.
cues: Navy leads 3–2 with one minute left.
F1 and F2 are visible support options.

questions.prompt: What lead and remaining time does the briefing state?

options.text: Navy trails 2–3
Navy leads 3–2 with one minute left
The clock is not stated

questions.explanation: The briefing states a one-goal Navy lead with one minute remaining.

questions.prompt: Which two cues affect the possession objective?

options.text: The stated lead and clock
F1 and F2's reachable support
The lead means every forward option is wrong

questions.explanation: The score and time shape risk, while support determines whether possession can be kept.

questions.prompt: Arrange a late-possession read.

options.text: Scan pressure and support
Protect or move the puck to a reachable option
Re-check whether the next lane remains safe

questions.explanation: The lead informs risk, but the actual support and pressure still decide the next action.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare routes toward F1 and F2.
questions.explanation: The example moves closer to F1 and F2, but also closer to Gold 1. Check pressure and both routes before treating either as a controlled outlet.

questions.prompt: F1 opens with room to retain the puck. What changes?

options.text: A controlled pass may reduce pressure while keeping possession
Force a shot because the lead is close
Dump without checking support

questions.explanation: F1 becoming reachable changes the safe-possession branch; the clock does not make one action automatic.

questions.prompt: Explain a sensible risk tradeoff without saying “never attack with a lead.”
questions.explanation: With a one-goal lead and one minute, value possession and support, but use a forward lane when it is clearly reachable and pressure leaves it available.

scenarios.title: Protect the backdoor during rotation
scenarios.objective: Exchange a low defensive responsibility while keeping the backdoor lane covered.
scenarios.briefing: Gold attacks Navy’s left net with four skaters against three in this penalty-kill example. Gold 1 controls behind the goal line and Gold 2 is across the low slot. YOU are on the side opposite the puck; D1 is on the puck side. The drill assigns YOU the low threat until a teammate confirms coverage. Gold 3 may cut inward in a later hypothetical.
cues: Gold 1 has the puck below the line.
Gold 2 is across the low slot.
YOU and D1 share a changing inside responsibility.

D1
YOU

questions.prompt: Which two checks belong before exchanging low responsibility?

options.text: D1's net-side position
Gold 2's route to the backdoor
The puck side fixes coverage forever

questions.explanation: Net-side support and the attacker route define the exchange; the rotation changes as Gold moves.

questions.prompt: Arrange a coverage handoff.

options.text: Identify puck and backdoor threat
Communicate the low exchange
Re-check the slot and net-side lane

questions.prompt: Compare a position closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2, opposite the puck side.
questions.explanation: The example is closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2 and opposite Gold 1. Check the low passing threat and D1 before assuming coverage is complete.

questions.prompt: Gold 2 receives below the line and Gold 3 cuts inward. What needs updating?

options.text: The low exchange and inside coverage
Stay on the original Gold 2 spot
Follow the puck without checking the slot

questions.explanation: Two attacker routes changed, so update who protects the inside and backdoor.

questions.prompt: Which low-slot passing threat should YOU track before exchanging coverage?
questions.explanation: Gold 2 starts across the low slot from carrier Gold 1. If Gold 3 cuts inward, update the threats and confirm the teammate exchange; a pass or coverage outcome is not guaranteed.
